The VisaNet Integrated Payment (V.I.P.) system supports full service processing, allowing clients worldwide to process point-of-sale and point-of-service (POS) transactions and automated teller machine (ATM) transactions. Full service processing is comprised of online functions, including authorization and financial messages and deferred clearing. VisaNet supports full service processing for the following cards in all regions (except as noted below):
Visa cards Cards bearing the Plus mark Cards bearing the Interlink or the Visa Interlink mark (Asia-Pacific [AP], Latin America and Caribbean [LAC], Visa Canada, and Visa U.S.A. regions only)

VisaNet also supports some non-Visa products in some countries. V.I.P. accepts all VisaNet messages from acquirers and from issuers. Clients can use a single connection for authorization, clearing, settlement, exception, and administrative messages.

Understanding full service processing requires a basic understanding of VisaNet and the interaction of its system components. This chapter provides a groundwork for understanding full service processing and financial messaging information, including:
A brief description of the VisaNet network and of its major systems. An overview of full service message processing and financial transactions. Brief summaries of related services.
A complete overview of VisaNet and of the V.I.P. System appears in the V.I.P. System Overview.

VisaNet is the Visa transaction processing network, supporting transactions routed among acquirers and issuers in Visa regions. VisaNet applies to the network’s hardware, software, and communications components and facilities, and client regional systems and networks. Main components of VisaNet are:
Visa Data Processing centers VisaNet telecommunications networks VisaNet connections: Direct Exchange (DEX), Visa Extended Access Server (EAS)
Note:  Clients in the Visa U.S.A. (U.S.) region access VisaNet through DEX. Clients in other Visa regions use DEX or EA servers.
Visa Merchant Direct Exchange (MDEX) and others, such as gateways to non-Visa destinations Processing centers

Visa Data Processing Centers (also known as VisaNet Interchange Centers or VICs) – House computer systems performing VisaNet transaction processing (such as authorization, clearing, and settlement) and that serve as control points for telecommunications facilities of VisaNet. Clients connect to VisaNet for transaction processing and file delivery. Visa data centers are linked globally, enabling each to serve as backup during system interruptions. Visa data processing centers (VICs) house the VisaNet Integrated Payment (V.I.P.) System. VisaNet Communications Network – Visa's super-resilient, highly-encrypted private (non-shared) network operates telecommunications lines and facilities worldwide to link users to Visa data processing centers and each other. Connections from one point in the network to another are not usually fixed links; instead, VisaNet chooses the best possible path at transmission time. Rerouting around failed lines occurs automatically. Links have multiple backups.

VisaNet Connection Methods – Visa provides reliable and protected network connectivity options for securely connecting directly to VisaNet, ensuring efficient acceptance and authorization of transactions, using V.I.P. message format:

Visa Extended Access Server (EAS) – Proprietary Visa endpoint access devices provide secure, managed access points for message processing and clearing file traffic to and from VisaNet. EASs leverage the Internet Protocol (IP) suite of communication protocols and other open-system technologies to provide secure client-site endpoint access.

Visa Direct Exchange (DEX) provides clients with one secure and extensible connection to VisaNet for message processing and file delivery. It uses two circuits and two carriers to ensure availability; each is configured to handle 100% of endpoints' projected transaction volume. If one circuit experiences problems, DEX switches traffic to the other circuit or carrier without degradation in service or interruption to processing. DEX components are:

Visa Message Gateway handles online transaction processing, resides at Visa data processing centers, and supports V.I.P. messages. It is a routing "switch" for V.I.P. transactions and controls traffic between VisaNet connections and Visa data processing centers. Open File Delivery (ODF) Service handles delivery of Automated Clearing House (ACH) data, BASE II data, Point-Of-Sale Authorization (POSA) File, and various reports and raw data. Note:  Clients in the U.S. region connect through DEX. Clients in other regions connect through EAS or DEX.
Clients can choose options for receiving reports and raw data and routing files. Options vary by region.

Visa Merchant Direct Exchange (MDEX) – Provides large merchants sponsored by their acquirer with direct access to VisaNet for message processing. MDEX uses either DEX or EAS. Processing Center – Processing centers (often called processors) are data processing facilities operated or designated by acquirers and issuers. Processing centers house systems supporting merchant and business locations and maintaining cardholder data and billing systems. Centers' host computers communicating with VisaNet connection methods must run computer interfaces to connections. Gateways to Non-Visa Destinations – If destinations are systems or networks outside of VisaNet, Gateway Services enables acquirers to obtain authorizations on non-Visa transactions through connections they use for Visa transactions. Acquirers and merchants can route transactions to VisaNet, which reformats messages for specific gateways and routes them to appropriate networks for responses. Gateway Services also enable issuers to use their VisaNet connections to receive requests from other networks or services.
V.I.P. is the primary transaction routing (switching) and processing system for online authorization and financial requests entering VisaNet. V.I.P. supports:

Authorization-only clients (clients that request transaction authorization in the first message, and financial clearing information in a second message which is processed through the BASE II system), and Full service clients (processing transactions containing authorization and clearing information in one full financial message and authorization and deferred clearing messages.)
The settlement process occurs separately. Clients can use different processing methods for different Visa Products (subject to Visa international and regional requirements.)

Full Service performs online cardholder transaction and exception processing, supports authorization and financial transactions and transaction delivery to BASE II for clients using authorization-only processing through V.I.P. (followed by a clearing transaction through BASE II.) Deferred clearing is where the final amount has not yet been confirmed and the advice which has yet to be received will contain the confirmed clearing amount. Full service processing passes activity data to VisaNet, which supports settlement and funds transfer processing for financial messages. VSS performs settlement and delivers results through advices and reports. V.I.P. supports full service POS transactions for:
Visa Interlink and Visa Interlink – although cardholders can use Interlink cards at ATMs to purchase stamps and sim
ilar items, V.I.P. treats these as POS transactions. Interlink is a POS-
only card product. Some non-Visa products

Full Financial Bridging A bridge from BASE II to full service endpoints creates a BASE II-generated advice to a full service issuer. A bridge from full service to authorization-only clients lets full service clients communicate with authorization-only clients and access authorization-only gateways.

Clearing is a processing service for the validation and valuation of financial and non-financial records exchanged between clients and Visa Services. The VisaNet Clearing system is referred to as BASE II. Clearing collects transactions from clients or processors, validates the information and values, calculates fees and charges as appropriate and then delivers it to the destination (other clients or processors.) A bridge to V.I.P. permits interchange between BASE II centers and full-service centers. Once transactions are cleared, they are ready for settlement. Clearing passes message data to the VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS), which settles with issuers and acquirers.

Settlement is the process of calculating and determining clients' net financial positions for transactions cleared by VisaNet. VSS consolidates settlement functions for cleared financial transactions into a single service for all products and services. VisaNet sends settlement information to clients and processors in standardized sets of reports. VSS offers flexibility in defining financial relationships, selecting reports and report destinations, and establishing funds transfer points. In a separate process, using the net position amounts provided by VSS, the Visa Treasury Management Department settles funds for the international settlement service with clients.

This section provides a brief description of the way a typical online full financial POS transaction with a personal identification number (PIN) flows from the merchant to the issuer and back, what occurs when the issuer system is not available, and what happens at the end of the processing day.
Full Service POS Message Transaction Flow

A cardholder swipes his or her card through a magnetic stripe reader. A terminal reads the chip on a card. A merchant manually enters the card number into a terminal. Contactless technology transmits the account number securely in a card-present situation without the need of a physical POS device such as a card reader or chip reader.

The customer may or may not enter a PIN; PINs are conditional in Visa POS transactions. Interlink and ATM transactions require PINs. 2. The merchant's acquirer takes the information and creates an 0100 authorization or 0200 full financial request message, logs
the event, and forwards the message to VisaNet.

3. V.I.P. logs and tracks the message, performs applicable message content editing, initiates service functions such as currency conversion, PIN, CVV, iCVV, dCVV verification, or CAVV validation, and routes the message to the issuer or processes the message in stand-in according to issuer availability and predetermined routing and stand-in-processing (STIP) parameters. 4. The issuer checks the transaction amount against the account's available balance and checks daily activity limits and other controls. The issuer logs the message and, for approved messages, reduces the cardholder's or customer's available balance by the amount of the transaction. The issuer creates an 0110 authorization or 0210 full financial response message based on the processing results and sends it to VisaNet. 5. V.I.P. logs the response and forwards it to the acquirer. 6. The acquirer logs the full financial response and forwards it to the point of sale or point of service (POS) to complete the transaction. The acquirer ensures it successfully delivers the response. V.I.P. settles the
transaction, if approved, after the next settlement cutoff time.
This figure illustrates how VisaNet processes an online financial transaction.

For Visa POS deferred-clearing purchases, acquirers can also use 0220 advices to submit purchase transactions. VisaNet authorizes deferred clearing transactions online and clears and settles them at a later time.

Although Visa designed V.I.P. to have issuers authorize transactions online, VisaNet has provisions to continue processing when the issuer's system is not available due to hardware, software, or communications failure. This stand-in processing (STIP) is available for all Visa transactions. It is available for some non-Visa card types depending on the region and issuer participation. STIP is not available for Mastercard transactions. While performing stand-in processing, V.I.P. can also verify the Card Verification Value (CVV), or the Integrated Chip Card card verification value (iCVV) for chip-based transactions, to detect the alteration of magnetic stripe or chip data. While performing stand-in processing, V.I.P. can also verify the Card Verification Value (CVV), the Integrated Chip Card card verification value (iCVV) or the Dynamic Card Verification Value (dCVV) for chip-based transactions, or validate the Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) in electronic-commerce transactions, to detect the alteration of magnetic stripe or chip data. Issuers can use the Positive Authorization Capacity Management (PACM) Service in conjunction with STIP to help them maximize their authorization and full financial message processing capacity. PACM monitors the issuer's transaction volume every 60 seconds. When the volume of authorization and full financial request messages exceeds the issuer's processing capacity, PACM routes low-risk transactions to STIP for the next minute. PACM continues to balance volume with capacity until the issuer is able to process all transactions. PACM creates advices with optional PACM indicators.

At settlement cutoff, VisaNet determines issuer and acquirer settlement positions and prepares daily reports and raw data files. Raw data files contain detailed information about the day's messages for a given participant. Similarly, issuers and acquirers use their internal transaction logs to account for the day's work and to prepare daily reports or files to reconcile to the reports and files they receive from VisaNet. The final step in the settlement process is funds transfer, during which VisaNet collects funds from settlement entities with net debit positions and pays funds to settlement entities with net credit positions. VisaNet provides V.I.P. full service users with a raw data file of all transactions. Clients can use this file to match transactions on a one-to-one basis to their systems' records to identify mismatched transactions and calculate settlement totals. Each client's operations staff reconcile data between VisaNet and the client, as well as the sponsored client, processor, or directly connected merchant. Operations staff compare the data from VisaNet against the client's internal transaction data to identify discrepancies. VisaNet includes a reporting facility producing daily and monthly reports for full service issuers and acquirers. The reports fall into two broad categories:
Transaction detail reports Settlement summary reports

Transaction detail reports contain details about the day's message activity. The detail reports list each transaction, including the settlement disposition. The detail reports also include reconciliation totals. Settlement summary reports contain summary information about the day's work. The summary reports provide totals for the various components including interchange totals and fee totals. VisaNet provides the Point-of-Sale Authorization (POSA) File to subscribing full service acquirers. The file contains transaction data and other authorization information improving billing accuracy and reducing fraud and dispute losses for acquirers. The POSA File provides a single daily file with debit and credit transaction data, contributing to increased operational efficiency. The file includes all of the data elements contained in the TC 33, SMS raw data records, and the POS reporting raw data and report files, besides providing additional data, such as card results-level data.
Clients can process all their POS transactions through a single connection as a full service endpoint. This section summarizes the following full service POS products:

VisaNet allows Visa POS and Interlink cardholders to purchase goods and services at participating merchant locations. To support these POS transactions, a client bank has the option to participate as a full service issuer, a full service acquirer, or as a full service issuer an d acquirer. In the online financial environment, full service clients use a single exchange of messages between the acquirer (or the directly connecte
d merchant) and the issuer to:
Authorize a financial transaction. Post a financial transaction to a cardholder's account. Post a financial transaction to a merchant's account. Settle funds between the acquirer and the issuer.
The purchase exchange consists of a request message from the acquirer, followed by a response message from the issuer.
Full Service POS Products for Acquirers

Full service allows acquirers to consistently process Visa, V PAY, and Interlink transactions for their merchants. If a client participates in multiple POS services, full service acquirers can use one message format and one connection to VisaNet. They can also use the same connection to support their full service ATM services.
Full service POS acquirers can process a full financial transaction in two ways:

They can authorize and clear POS transactions by submitting a single online full financial message to VisaNet. This function occurs when the acquirer knows the final purchase amount at the time o f authorization. They can authorize transactions online and submit an online full financial message through VisaNet at a later time. This
deferred function occurs when the acquirer does not know the
final purchase amount at the time of authorization. This method of processing differs depending on the POS card program:

Visa POS acquirers can use online deferred clearing processing. Interlink acquirers can preauthorize Interlink transactions and submit an online full financial message through VisaNet within two hours. The Interlink preauthorization transaction is an online full financial transaction set involving a preauthorization transaction followed by a second clearing, or completion, transaction.
Acquirers serve as the points of interaction between the merchants and VisaNet. Visa requires acquirers:

Support the acquirer transaction set. Log all financial and non-financial transactions (approved or declined) and all postings to merchant accounts. Forward responses to the POS device and determine successful delivery of responses. Assure total system security of cardholders' PINs. PIN usage is conditional for Visa POS, but Visa requires it for Interlink. See
Payment Technology Standards Manual for information

about PIN security and conditional usage. Process exception transactions (initiate adjustments and dispute response financials and receive dispute financial responses.) Send and receive administrative messages.
Full Service POS Products for Issuers

Participating issuers can process Visa POS and Interlink transactions using one message format and one connection to the V.I.P. system. They can also use the same connection to support their full service ATM services. Full service POS issuers can immediately authorize and post online financial transactions received from full service POS acquirers. In addition, Visa POS issuers must have the ability to authorize transactions online and to receive online deferred clearing transactions through V.I.P. at a later time. For batch-deferred clearing transactions from authorization-only/BASE II Visa POS acquirers or for online-deferred clearing transactions from full service acquirers, issuers receive the authorization message at the time of purchase and the clearing message later.

VisaNet delivers the authorization and clearing messages through the issuer's full service VisaNet connection, enabling the issuer to maintain one consistent method for processing all Visa-branded products. The main function of issuers' systems is to accurately respond, based on cardholders' accounts and PINs, to messages received from the V.I.P. System. Issuers also must send dispute financials, administrative messages, and network management messages. Issuers receive transaction requests and approve or decline them based on predefined parameters. Visa requires issuers:

Support the full complement of POS transactions for Visa. Approve or decline all full financial transaction requests. Receive advices from the stand-in processor (STIP). Log all transactions. Initiate dispute financial responses and receive adjustments and dispute response financials. Send and receive administrative messages.
This section identifies the services that V.I.P. full service supports. See V.I.P. System Services.

Routing refers to sending messages between VisaNet and acquirer and issuer processing centers. Routing also refers to issuer-specified conditions triggering Visa stand-in processing (STIP) to authorize a transaction on an issuer's behalf. Visa assumes responsibility for routing a request to its proper destination. For instance, acquirers do not have to determine the destination of their authorization or financial requests because V.I.P. routes requests based on the account number in the message. In some cases, V.I.P. uses data other than the account number to determine message routing. Issuers designate which of their issuer processing centers should receive the requests. The issuer associates each issuing identifier (a range of card numbers for a specific card program, such as Visa Classic) with a specific issuer processing center. Optionally, issuers can control which processing center receives requests for their cardholders by designating multiple processing centers and specifying the types of transactions VisaNet should route to each processing center. In addition to basic routing functionality, Visa provides a variety of routing services enabling issuers and acquirers to specify alternate routing for transactions with specified characteristics. Most of the routing services V.I.P. provides are optional. Issuers can designate an alternate path for routing particular transaction types. For instance, issuers can route POS transactions differently from ATM
transactions; they can route PIN transactions differently from non-PIN transactions; they can route exception transactions differently from authorizations and financial transactions.

The ATM/POS Split Routing Service enables issuers processing Visa and Plus transactions to separate types of transactions and to accept or to route these transactions to or from two or more processing endpoints. The service offers the following options:

The ATM/POS Split Routing option allows acquirers and issuers to use separate processing centers for ATM and POS transactions. The ATM/POS Account-Type Split Routing option is available to issuers processing ATM transactions. The POS option supports POS and multipurpose card transactions for full service and authorization-only issuers in the Asia-Pacific (AP) region only. This routing option allows issuers to direct V.I.P. to route ATM transactions based on the account the cardholder selects when using a multipurpose card at an ATM. Authorization-only and full service issuers in the AP region can have VisaNet route POS transactions based on the account the cardholder selects when using a multipurpose card at the POS. Issuers can specify two endpoints: one for deposit account processing, and one for credit account processing. The Alternate Routing option is available to full service acquirers and issuers. This option allows full service entities to choose separate routing for certain transaction types, including exception items and other back-office transactions. Issuers and acquirers may designate their primary processing center to process online original transactions and one or more alternate processing centers to process exception and back-office transactions.

The V.I.P. System has connections, or gateways, to various systems and networks. V.I.P. is connected with the Cirrus Gateway (V.I.P. Network 0006) and the Mastercard Gateway (V.I.P. Network 0007) through the Mastercard Debit Switch (M.D.S.) for the exchange of transactions for ATM processing. This gateway supports chip and multicurrency processing. V.I.P. generates 0620 Mobile IP Gateway Notification Advices for cardholders. Issuers can choose to receive notification advices. V.I.P. does not create these types of advices for balance-only alerts sent to cardholders. Gateway Services link acquirers accepting non-Visa card products and services to other networks outside of VisaNet using the same connections they use for Visa transactions.
This service enables issuers to separate message traffic according to the following options:

The PIN/No-PIN Split Routing option enables issuers to separate transaction message traffic requiring PINs from message traffic not requiring PINs (called “no-PIN transactions”). POS with PIN transactions have the option of being routed to an alternate endpoint for POS transactions without a PIN.

This service allows full service acquirers accepting more than one card brand (or mark) to assign each of them a priority. Prioritization enables V.I.P. to determine the actual network and set of program rules to use for each transaction. The Priority Routing Service does not require the acquirer to assign a specific network identifier to a transaction. Clients can use the Priority Routing Service with the Alternate Routing option. Clients can also use the Priority Routing Service to prioritize non-Visa programs destined for VisaNet gateways to other systems and networks provided by Gateway Services.

Visa offers the following online request services full service participants can use. (Unless otherwise indicated, see V.I.P. System Services, for comprehensive descriptions of all of the services summarized in this chapter.)

The Account Verification Service enables merchants to request an account number verification as an initial check for an estimated purchase. V.I.P. supports requests for account number information through the Account Verification Service.

The Address Verification Service (AVS) is an online Visa service enabling merchants to reduce fraud losses by verifying cardholders' billing addresses for card-not-present (CNP) transactions. Participants can use AVS for Visa, American Express, and Discover transactions, and Mastercard POS transactions. STIP performs address verification for Visa and proprietary and private-label transactions only.

Field 3—Pr 3—Processing Code, positions 1–2, contains 39 (eligibility message). Field 25 25—Point-of-Service Condition Code contains 51 (zero amount account verification). Field 52—PIN Data and Field 53—Security-Related Control Information are present, or Field 123—Verification Data is present, or Field 126.10—CVV2 Authorization Request Data is present.

Also, field 4 can be zero in 0302 file update requests or 9620 fraud advice requests. If the request meets all the verification-only field requirements, and field 4 contains an amount other than zero,
STIP ignores the amount and, if the request is successful, responds with a value of 85 (no reason to decline) in field 39.

Visa Advanced Authorization provides transaction risk assessment to issuers for Visa card cardholders during the POS and ATM authorization request process. Visa Advanced Authorization is required for U.S. issuers and is a subscription-based service for issuers in Visa Canada and the Asia- Pacific (AP), Latin America and Caribbean (LAC), and Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East, and Africa (CEMEA) regions. To receive the Visa Advanced Authorization fields, Field 62.21—Advanced Authorization Risk Score and Field 62.22—Advanced Authorization Condition Code, in an authorization request, the issuer must first successfully complete testing. Issuers can optionally include Visa Advanced Authorization risk score threshholds as part of their STIP processing parameters.

The Automatic Cardholder Database Update (Auto-CDB) Service enables V.I.P. to update records in the Exception File when issuers return a pick-up response code in authorization response messages. The Auto-CDB Service helps issuers prevent losses from problem accounts and improves the accuracy of cardholder information available to V.I.P. for stand-in processing (STIP). The Auto-CDB Service is not available for Interlink. For details about this service, refer to V.I.P. System Services.
Card Verification Value (CVV) Service, the Integrated Chip Card Card Verification Value (iCVV), and the Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) Service
Issuers can choose to have the Visa Security Module (VSM) verify the following verification values all of the time or only when the issuer is unavailable and STIP processes the transaction.

A card verification value (CVV) is a 3-digit number encoded on the card's physical magnetic stripe or in the chip's image on a Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) card. An Integrated Chip Card card verification value (iCVV) is a 3-digit number issuers may encode in the chip's image on a VSDC chip card instead of the CVV. (The iCVV is also referred to as the alternate CVV.) A VSDC card's chip image may contain the CVV or iCVV. A card's physical magnetic stripe does not use an iCVV. The Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) is an embossed 3-digit security number appearing on the reverse side of the card. A customized option is also allowed for placement of the CVV2 on standard Visa cards. The CVV2 may be printed directly on the card background, on either the front or back of the card. Clients can use the CVV2 in card-present and card-not-present transactions.
Visa offers a verification service for the following:
Card Verification Value (CVV or iCVV) for card-present transactions. Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) for card-present and card-not-present transactions.

The CPS/Account Funding program requirements include the CVV2 for electronic commerce (e- commerce) stored-value transactions. For stored-value cards refilled more than once, the program requires the CVV2 only in the initial funding request for the request to qualify; subsequent transactions can qualify for the CPS program without the CVV2 being present. To verify the CVV, V.I.P. (or the issuer) uses the DES key and other information from the stripe to calculate a CVV and compares it with the stripe's encoded CVV. For the CVV to be valid, the two values must match exactly; otherwise, the CVV fails validation. As indicated above, iCVV processing uses all options, parameters, and keys used in CVV processing. V.I.P. or the issuer uses the same algorithm for the CVV and for the iCVV, but they substitute the

value 999 for the service restriction code for iCVV processing. As part of the issuer participation procedure, the issuer specifies expiration date ranges and whether the CVV check is to be based on the chip image of the magnetic stripe data. The Card Verification Value 2 (CVV2) Service is a card verification tool designed to reduce fraud losses on card-present and card-not-present transactions. Issuers must imprint a 3-digit security number (the CVV2) on the front or back of all new or reissued Visa cards, in accordance with the Visa Rules. Clients can use the CVV2 number to validate a genuine Visa card is used during a transaction. The CVV2 is calculated using a secure cryptographic process and a key known only to the issuer and to Visa. Participating merchants manually enter the CVV2 numeric value for validation by the V.I.P. System, the issuer, or both. V.I.P., the issuer, or both, verifies the CVV2 and returns the CVV2 result code to the merchant. Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) Verification Service and Electronic Commerce Transactions

The Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) Verification Service is a risk control service used to authenticate the cardholder in electronic commerce (e-commerce) authorization transactions. The process involves two phases: 1.
Visa Secure (formerly known as Verified by Visa (VbV)) 2. CAVV Verification Service

During the Visa Secure phase, the cardholder is electronically identified and a CAVV is generated associated with the purchase. The CAVV Verification Service processing begins when the acquirer submits the authorization or the full financial message and includes the CAVV (in Field 126.9—CAVV Data) generated during the Visa Secure phase in the request. When the CAVV is present in the transaction, the issuer or V.I.P. verifies the CAVV in the message matches the CAVV generated during the Visa Secure phase. If V.I.P. or the

issuer verifies the CAVV, the transaction is protected from certain chargebacks should disputes arise later. When the issuer or V.I.P. (depending on who performed the validation), completes the validation process, it places the results in Field 44.13—Card Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) Result Code. The value in this field indicates the outcome of the validation, where the validation was performed, and the classification of the transaction: Authentication, Attempt, or Non-Secure. To validate the CAVV, the issuer or V.I.P. on behalf of the issuer, uses Data Encryption Standard (DES) keys and other CAVV parameters to calculate the CAVV and compare it to the CAVV generated by the Access Control Server (ACS). Issuers choosing to have V.I.P. perform verification on their behalf must provide Visa with their DES keys. Visa offers two classifications of CAVV Verification Service processing options to issuers participating in Visa Secure: Authentication or Attempt. Visa encourages issuers to participate in both. Authentication—With this option, the issuer is a full participant in the service and has cardholders enrolled in Visa Secure. Visa classifies a transaction as an Authentication when the acquirer, the issuer, and the cardholder all participate in Visa Secure. Attempt—With this option, the issuer or V.I.P. generates a CAVV for attempted transactions. Visa classifies a transaction submitted by a participating acquirer as an Attempt when the issuer or cardholder does not participate in Visa Secure. Liability shifts for these types of transactions. This option is mandatory in some regions. Both options allow issuers to select a predefined process by which their transactions should be processed by the issuer and by STIP. The predefined processes are as follows:

Standard Issuer CAVV Service/Standard Decline/Failure option, with which V.I.P. performs all validations on the issuer's behalf, declines transactions when the CAVV validation fails, and forwards the status results of transactions it doesn’t decline to the issuer. All CAVV Verification Results to the Issuer option, with which VisaNet performs all validations on the issuer's behalf, and forwards all status results of transactions to the issuer. Issuer Supports Own CAVV Verification option, with which VisaNet forwards the transactions to the issuer to perform validation. The issuer returns the status results in the response messages.

Depending on the region, VisaNet assesses interchange reimbursement fees (IRFs) based on the CAVV Verification Service classification of the e-commerce transaction. The CAVV Verification Service supports magnetic stripe Visa cards and Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) cards. The PIN Verification Service (PVS) is a V.I.P. service providing full-time or stand-in verification of personal identification numbers (PINs) used for Visa and Plus ATM transactions, for Visa point of service (POS) and Interlink POS transactions, and for Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) transactions. A personal identification number is a secret code identifying a cardholder at an ATM or at a terminal. A PIN serves as an electronic substitute for a cardholder's signature. At the issuer's option, the V.I.P. System can verify PINs on behalf of the issuer center at all times or only when the center is unavailable. When V.I.P. verifies PINs, it intercepts all authorization requests containing PINs, verifies the PINs, and passes the requests to the issuers or to the V.I.P. stand-in processor (STIP) for authorization processing.

Participation in PVS is optional for Visa issuers, Plus issuers, Interlink issuers, VSDC issuers, and issuers of all other card products. V.I.P. must perform PIN translation for Interlink issuers. However, Interlink issuers can perform PIN verification or can have V.I.P. provide this service at the issuer's option. For more information, see V.I.P. System Services.

The Positive Authorization Capacity Management (PACM) Service helps issuers maximize their authorization and full financial message processing capacity. PACM monitors the issuer's transaction volume every 60 seconds. When the volume of authorization and financial request messages exceeds the issuer's processing capacity, PACM routes low-risk transactions to stand-in processing (STIP) for the next minute. PACM continues to balance volume with capacity until the issuer is able to process all transactions. PACM creates advices with optional PACM indicators.
Activation, Load, and Partial Approval Processing

V.I.P. processes cards for Visa and private-label card products, as well as for Interlink. Merchants and issuers submit transactions to activate cards and to load spending amounts onto activated cards. They can also submit load requests without submitting activation requests, and can activate and load value to cards in a single request message. In the U.S. and Canada regions, the Visa ReadyLink Service activates and loads Visa cards through VisaNet. The ReadyLink Service supports electronic fare load transactions, which enable chip cards to be used for contactless access to a transit system. U.S. acquirers choosing to support these transactions must be able to send the access token account number for the cardholder's chip card in field 102. U.S. issuers choosing to support these transactions must be able to receive field 102. When merchants submit authorizations for an amount greater than the amount loaded onto the card, issuers can return partial authorizations for the available amount on the card. An emergency shutoff flag in V.I.P. shields POS-load issuers from receiving ATM loads. Merchants and issuers submit activation or load void requests, or reversals, for cards activated or loaded in error. Merchants and issuers can submit a void only on the same day as the original request. Prepaid transactions, including partial authorizations, are eligible for STIP. Participation in prepaid card processing services is optional for issuers, acquirers, processors, and merchants. Visa requires acquirers participating in prepaid transactions to support partial approval amounts. Visa requires issuers participating in prepaid transactions to support the partial authorization value in request messages, but may optionally support partial authorization responses. Acquirers and issuers must complete testing for sending and receiving prepaid transactions.

Contactless transactions are made using contactless chip Visa cards. The Dynamic Card Verification Value (dCVV) resides in the contactless card. dCVV verification processing occurs when a terminal (or contactless device) equipped to accept contactless chip cards reads the chip card. The contactless chip creates the dCVV value and inserts it into the Track 1 or Track 2 magnetic stripe data it transmits to the terminal along with other data. The dCVV replaces CVV data in track data. Visa contactless cards are one of the following:
A magnetic stripe Visa card with an embedded contactless chip. A Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) chip card having a magnetic stripe and supporting contactless chip.

Clients accepting and processing VSDC chip cards for contactless transactions must be participants in the VSDC Service. A card can include a contactless chip with its dCVV algorithm as well as a CVV in the Track 1 or Track 2 magnetic stripe. A VSDC chip card can also contain a contactless chip, with its dCVV algorithm, as well as a CVV or an iCVV. V.I.P. identifies a contactless authorization or financial request if the POS entry mode code in field 22 is 07 (contactless chip transaction originated using VSDC chip data rules) or is 91 (contactless chip using magnetic stripe data rules). VisaNet supports the use of contactless chip cards for ATM transactions. Additionally, in the United States (U.S.) region, acquirers must insert code 8 in Field 60.2—Terminal Entry Capability. Acquirers in other regions do not have to use code 8 in field 60.2 V.I.P. supports contactless chip cards having an alternative primary account number (PAN) stored on the chip. This PAN is different from the PAN embossed on the card; it serves as a security measure to prevent counterfeit chip cards from being used for non-chip transactions. Alternative PAN processing applies to contactless chip cards using qVSDC, VSDC, and magnetic stripe data. V.I.P. account ranges can be set up to indicate alternative PAN support. V.I.P. declines a transaction with response code 59 (suspected fraud) if all of the following apply:
The account range of the card indicates it supports an alternative PAN. Field 22 does not contain 05, 07, 91, or 95. Chip data is not present in field 55 or the third bitmap fields.

Visa Contactless ATM Transactions—V.I.P supports Visa contactless ATM transactions in network 0002 and network 0004. Acquirers implementing Visa contactless ATM transactions must support full chip data. Acquirers implementing these transactions for the first time must use full chip data in Field 55, Usage 1 – VSDC Chip Data. However, acquirers using the expanded third bitmap format can continue to use their format for processing Visa contactless ATM transactions. A recurring payment transaction is one occurring on a periodic basis per an agreement between the cardholder and the merchant for payments for goods and services such as utility bills and magazine or online subscriptions. The initial transaction can occur in card-present (face-to-face POS) or card- not-present (MOTO or e-commerce) environments. Merchants automatically initiate subsequent, or recurring, transactions without the cardholder being notified beforehand or necessarily being present. The presence of 02 in Field 60.8—Positions 9–10, Mail/Phone/Electronic Commerce Payment Indicator or R in Field 126.13—POS Environment identifies the transaction as a recurring payment authorization request. 02 in field 60.8, positions 9–10, is mandatory for recurring payment transactions acquired in the U.S. region and is optional for non-U.S.-acquired transactions. recurring payment transactions originating from an acquirer outside of the U.S. region. Use of this value is optional for U.S.-acquired transactions. Depending on the region, acquirers may send both fields with their recurring payment codes in the same request. Fields and their values are valid for dispute protection. If the issuer has not successfully completed testing to receive field 126.13, V.I.P. drops it before forwarding the request to the issuer and inserts code 02 in field 60.8. The Trusted Agent Program (TAP), formerly called the Visa Agent Identification Service (AIS), informs acquirers of merchants using unregistered agents (including third-party servicers and merchant servicers) to submit transactions to VisaNet using the acquiring identifiers. Unauthorized VisaNet access compromises the security of the Visa payment system and exposes Visa clients to considerable risk from theft and fraud. Although acquirers are financially liable for all transactions submitted under their acquiring identifiers, they are often unaware of the merchant-agent arrangements because the transactions pass through agents to VisaNet, bypassing the acquirer. TAP greatly reduces acquirers’ risk by monitoring transactions submitted through acquiring agents to VisaNet and reporting unauthorized use of acquiring identifiers to acquirers. TAP identifies unregistered agents and logs them for acquirer registration and Visa risk analysis. TAP applies to all POS 0100 and 0200 authorization and full financial request messages processed through V.I.P. (including Interlink.) Visa assigns each agent a secret code and unique ID. When an agent receives a request from a merchant, the agent constructs the contents of Field 126 – Agent Unique Account Result (AUAR), by hashing the secret code, unique ID, and the account number according to a Visa-specified

algorithm. The agent forwards the AUAR to the acquiring VisaNet processor along with the other merchant information for submission to VisaNet. If an acquiring processor receives the merchant's authorization request or full financial request message from the agent but the agent did not include the AUAR, the acquiring processor uses a Visa-supplied default AUAR for the VisaNet submission. If an acquiring processor receives requests directly from a merchant, field 126.18 is not required and must not be present in the request. V.I.P. does not edit the field; it also does not send it to the issuer processor nor does it return field 126.18 in the response. VisaNet validates the field offline and sends summary reports to the acquirers or to their designates. Currently, U.S. acquirers and their processors can optionally support TAP. They can test now to send field 126.18.
Visa will require all U.S. acquirer processors to support TAP at a later date.
Visa Cashback Processing: VisaNet Cashback Service

The VisaNet Cashback Service provides domestic cashback transaction capability for participating regions. A domestic cashback transaction is one for which the merchant, acquirer, and the issuer are in the same country. Regions can choose to implement cashback processing capability as a domestic-specific solution without VisaNet, or they can participate in the VisaNet Cashback Service. Cashback processing is optional for issuers, for acquirers, and for merchants in all Visa regions. Participating regions and countries within those regions establish maximum cashback amounts. Regions using the VisaNet Cashback Service can control client and country participation, and can set maximum cashback limits and different pricing options by country. Acquirers and acquirer processors in the U.S. region, and those in the AP and LAC regions with merchants in U.S. territories, processing Visa and Interlink POS transactions with cashback must support partial authorizations. U.S. issuers are not permitted to partially approve cashback amounts requested by the cardholder as part of a purchase transaction. V.I.P. checks the acquiring and issuing identifiers, the acquirer country code in field 19, and the merchant country code in field 43 to determine if the POS cashback transaction is domestic. The cashback amount field is Field 61.1—Other Amounts. If the transaction is non-domestic, V.I.P. converts the cashback amount in field 61.1 to the issuer currency code and forwards the converted amount in field 61.2 to the issuer. Purchase transactions with cashback receiving partial authorization from the issuer must be approved only for the amount of the merchandise. Issuers must not approve portions of the cashback amount.

Visa Secure Electronic Commerce (VSEC) With Visa Secure

The Visa Secure Electronic Commerce (VSEC) initiative provides security for transactions sent over the Internet and over other open networks. Implemented as part of the VSEC initiative, Visa has developed technology to authenticate the cardholder during an online purchase. The authentication technology is called 3-D Secure; the authentication service available to cardholders is referred to as Visa Secure (formerly known as Verified by Visa (VbV)). Participation in Visa Secure is mandatory for acquirers with electronic commerce merchants. Each region determines requirements for issuer participation in Visa Secure.

Visa Smart Debit/Smart Credit (VSDC) is a chip-based Visa card product supporting offline and online transactions, including Plus ATM transactions. VSDC cards work in conjunction with special chip-read terminals to approve or to decline transactions. VSDC offline transactions occur only between the cardholder's chip card and the terminal and do not go through VisaNet. VisaNet processes transactions online when processing triggers predetermined offline risk management procedures, or because of random selection parameters established by the issuer. For purchase transactions, the issuer may determine whether a cardholder signature or a PIN is required for cardholder verification. ATM transactions require a PIN. VSDC cards rely on cryptograms to ensure their security and the integrity of their offline and online transactions. Issuers selecting the Full Data implementation option verify the cryptogram submitted by Full Data acquirers in the 0100 authorization request. The card terminal authenticates the issuer's cryptogram in the 0110 authorization response to ensure the issuer that created the card is the issuer that approved the transaction. If V.I.P. performs processing for the Card Authentication feature on behalf of the issuer, V.I.P. validates the Authorization Request Cryptogram (ARQC) and provides the Authorization Response Cryptogram (ARPC) in the response. If the issuer participates in the Issuer Authentication feature, the issuer or V.I.P. generates a cryptogram (Authorization Response Cryptogram) sent to the card in the response so the card can validate the authorization response came from the correct issuer. Issuer participation is optional in the VSDC Card Authentication feature and in the Issuer Authentication feature. V.I.P. identifies a VSDC-based authorization request by the value in Field 22—Point-of-Service Entry Mode Code indicating a chip card was read at a VSDC terminal (05 or 95) and the service restriction code in the magnetic stripe is 2 (international card, alternate technology) or is

alternate technology). V.I.P. processes VSDC transactions according to card type. VisaNet supports the following card types: Visa Integrated Circuit Card Specification (VIS)—This card type uses the initial Visa chip card type specifications for communicating between EMV (JCB, Mastercard, Visa) cards and their issuer processors.

Common Core Definition (CCD)—CCD is a newer EMV card type containing the same data as a VIS card but in a more flexible message format transmitting more chip data. Generic EMV Transport—This card type is also EMV-compliant but carries issuer-defined online chip information not processed by VisaNet. V.I.P. tr treats Generic EMV Transport transactions as “pass- through” transactions, valid for PIN translation but ineligible for field edit, Visa chip or issuer authentication services, or STIP. Acquirers processing transactions in America Express U.S. territories must support American Express EMV chip-based contact and contactless transactions. Acquirers processing transactions in American Express Caribbean and Central and South American regions must support American Express EMV chip-based contact transactions. For details of American Express regions, refer to the American Express documentation. V.I.P. supports chip cards having an alternative primary account number (PAN) stored on the chip. Visa iCVV Convert is available for authorization-only and full service users, and also supports contactless chip transactions. For participating issuers, VisaNet makes changes to the following fields before forwarding the authorization request:

Field 60.3 (Chip Condition Code), Field 60.6 (Chip Transaction Indicator), and Field 60.7 (Chip Card Authentication Reliability Indicator) are zero-filled, or dropped, if no subsequent field 60 subfields are present. Field 39—VisaNet does not send Online CAM authentication results (response code

However, the response codes Y1, Y2, Z1 and Z3 are sent in 0120/0220 advices to participating issuers. CVV results are sent in field 44.5.

If the issuer participates in Visa iCVV Convert and the transaction passes Online Card Authentication Method (Online CAM), VisaNet replaces the iCVV present in the track data (field 35 or field 45) with a VisaNet-generated CVV. However, if the transaction fails iCVV validation, VisaNet declines the transaction with response code 05 (do not honor). VisaNet declines the transaction with response code 05 (do not honor) if the issuer participates in Visa iCVV Convert, but the issuer's MDK (Online CAM) and CVK (CVV) are not present.

Visa offers the following tools to issuers and to acquirers enabling them to minimize their exposure to fraud. Most of the risk services are optional.

The Card Recovery Bulletin (CRB) Service is an international risk control service maintaining card recovery files containing account numbers of cards reported as lost, stolen, or misused. It maintains card recovery files (including the CD-ROM bulletin) for most acquirers, and merchant mailing files for all acquirers. It also helps control fraud on below-floor-limit transactions outside of the U.S. region. The CRB Service protects cardholders from fraudulent use of their lost or stolen cards. It also supports dispute rights of issuers, acquirers, merchants, and cardholders.

The Fraud Reporting System (FRS) is a V.I.P. service helping clients report, track, and analyze fraudulent transactions. FRS consolidates fraud information, helping clients detect fraud patterns and reduce losses.

Visa requires clients to electronically report confirmed fraud transactions on all Visa cards. Acquirers and issuers must comply with the fraud reporting rules as defined in Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules. The Online Fraud Reporting option, available through V.I.P., allows full service clients to report fraud using full financial advice messages.

This service provides participating acquirers and their e-commerce merchants with the Visa Transaction Advisor (VTA) e- commerce risk score and risk condition code. Acquirers and their e-commerce merchants can use this information in assessing transaction risk when deciding whether to proceed with a transaction. In order for an e-commerce transaction to receive the VTA e-commerce risk score and risk condition code, the PCR for the acquiring identifier and the MVV must be set up to participate in the Visa Transaction Advisor E-Commerce Scoring Service. Acquirers participating in the Visa Transaction Advisor E-Commerce Scoring Service must be able to receive Field 104, Usage 2 – Transaction-Specific Data, with Dataset ID 5B – Visa Risk Assessment Data, in approved 0110 Authorization response and 0210 Full financial response messages. For more information, contact your regional client support representative.

The Account Funding Service allows Visa cardholders to fund accounts such as brokerage accounts and accounts associated with stored value cards. The Account Funding Service uses CVV2s as a cardholder risk control measure, which is one of the requirements for an electronic commerce (e- commerce) stored-value card transaction to qualify for the CPS/Account Funding Program. For stored-value cards to be refilled more than once, the CVV2 is required only in the initial funding request for the request to qualify; subsequent transactions can also qualify for the CPS program without the CVV2 being present.
The Chargeback Reduction Service (CRS) is designed to:
Reduce client costs by eliminating unnecessary exception items. Improve the accuracy and timeliness of valid exception transactions.
CRS applies to Visa only—not to ATM or Interlink.

The VisaNet Copy Request and Fulfillment Service (VCRFS) facilitates the process of requesting and delivering copies of sales drafts between clients and merchants. In addition, VCRFS permits Visa to perform compliance monitoring, while reducing costs and increasing customer satisfaction. The goal of this service is to fully automate all copy request fulfillments based on client needs and cost effectiveness. The Visa Mobile Prepaid (VMP) service allows financially underserved consumers in emerging markets to gain access to interoperable financial services. VMP uses mobile money accounts to turn cash into digital currency that can be used in financial transactions such as purchasing, paying bills, buying airtime, sending funds to acquaintances, or loading or withdrawing funds. VMP transactions are supported in certain countries within the Visa AP, Visa CEMEA, and Visa LAC regions only. Contact your Visa representative for more information. VMP accounts can be used for the following:

Agent Cash In: Cash in transactions enable the addition of money to a mobile money account using OCTs. Agent Cash Out: Cash out transactions enable withdrawal of funds from a mobile money account. Agent Cash Claim: Cash claim transactions enable withdrawal of funds from a mobile money account using a manual cash transaction. Agent Bill Pay: Bill pay transactions enable withdrawal of funds from a mobile money account using AFTs to pay bills or make airtime top up purchases. Person-to-Person (P2P) Money Transfer: P2P money transfer enable sending and receiving of funds to a mobile money account using an OCT. Purchase and ATM: VMP accounts can be used for retail purchases, including electronic commerce. Transactions can be initiated at ATMs. Bulk Business-to-Consumer (B2C) Funds Disbursement Transactions.

The Visa Token Service provides clients enhanced protection against counterfeit, account misuse, and other forms of fraud in card-not-present and hybrid transaction environments. This service helps to minimize unauthorized use of cardholder account data in a transaction. The Visa Token Service uses the EMV Payment Tokenization Specification–Technical Framework (payment token framework) published by EMVCo addressing processing considerations and use of payment tokens to protect cardholder payment credentials. Visa Token Service allow acquirers, merchants, and digital wallet

providers to request for tokens. Tokens are surrogate values which replaces the PAN in transaction processing. Token vaults generate and store tokens along with their associated PANs and issue them when requested. Token service providers operate token vaults. Token requestors can request tokens at different stages of the transaction including authorization, capture, clearing, and exception processing. The PAN is never passed in the transaction when a token is requested, this enhances the security during transaction processing. VisaNet supports token provisioning, payment processing, and lifecycle management for:

Secure Element (SE) mobile devices: Visa contactless for mobile transactions require account credentials to be stored in a secure chip on the mobile device called the secure element (SE). It is a physical element placed on the mobile device by the manufacturer. Visa Token Service enables token usage for consumer mobile devices supporting secure element (SE). This option allows using tokens for near field communication (NFC) Visa contactless POS transactions and application-based e-commerce transaction processing with SE consumer device-issued payment tokens. Host Card Emulation (HCE) mobile devices: Visa cloud-based payments program provides issuers to support Visa contactless for mobile transactions even without a secured element placed on the mobile device. Issuers can provide consumers mobile payment capabilities with a range of Visa-approved host card emulation (HCE)-capable mobile devices. Major operating systems like Google Android™ supports HCE. HCE environment allows applications in the mobile device to directly use the NFC capabilities and communicate with a merchant’s contactless terminal. Merchants can also accept mobile payments in-store using Visa contactless infrastructure or other technology interfaces available. Card-on-File (COF): Acquirers and their merchants can request a token to replace the cardholder primary account number (PAN). The acquirer card-on-file token provisioning allows acquirers and their merchants to request a payment token. Once the acquirer has obtained the token, acquirer card-on-file token processing allows acquirers and their merchants to process the transaction using the token instead of the cardholder PAN. The acquirer will use the token instead of the cardholder PAN for transactions, such as card-not- present transactions, when POS authorizations are initiated and when clearing transaction processing takes place.
For more information, contact your regional client support representative.
Fees and charges for full service users are collected daily through the daily settlement process or monthly through Visa's monthly billing process.
A fee is a vehicle for passing costs between clients. An interchange reimbursement fee (IRF) is an example of a fee. Fees are paid by the acquirer to the issuer or by the issuer to the acquirer.

There are three types of interchange reimbursement fees (IRFs). Domestic Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in the same country. Intraregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different countries within the same Visa region. Interregional Interchange Reimbursement Fees—Fees paid by one participant to another for transactions acquired and issued in different Visa regions. In this context, transaction country is the country in which the transaction takes place, and issuing country is the country of the issuer of the card used in the transaction. If no domestic IRF has been established, the intraregional IRF applies. If no intraregional IRF has been established, the interregional (international) IRF applies. IRFs are settled daily through the settlement process. For National Net Settlement Service transactions, there is only one settlement currency, so balancing does not involve currency conversion. For International Settlement Service transactions, however, there are many settlement currencies. Visa uses buy and sell rates for currency conversion. These rates are paired into USD-based rates used when converting non-USD currencies against the U.S. dollar, and cross-rates (non-USD-based rates) used for selected currencies in which the rates quoted are against a currency other than the U.S. dollar. The Multicurrency Service automatically converts the transaction currency to the acquirer's settlement currency (if the two are different), and automatically converts the cardholder's billing currency to the issuer's settlement currency (if the two are different), to one of the settlement currencies. For POS transactions, IRFs are typically paid by acquirers to issuers. Fees for manual cash disbursements, reversals, merchandise returns, dispute financials, and credit adjustments flow in the opposite direction. Interlink transactions from merchants having MCCs other than the eligible codes receive non-tiered Interlink rates based on transaction qualifications.
Some fees are passed between a client and Visa. Access and Use Fees—These fees are for clients and processors directly connected to VisaNet.

A charge is a vehicle used to bill clients for Visa processing costs. There are transaction processing charges, administrative and service charges, and cross border charges. A charge can be issuer- or acquirer-unique or it can apply to both. The charge paid by the client is credited to the client's Visa region. Charging requirements vary by region and are subject to approval by the regional board. Each region establishes the specific criteria by which its charges are assessed.
Transaction processing charges are assessed by Visa to issuers and acquirers for transactions processed through VisaNet. These charges, which may vary by transaction type, are billed monthly.
Administrative and service charges include: Most administrative and service charges are billed monthly.

The International Service Assessment (ISA) is applied to both issuers and acquirers on all cash and sales transactions, where the merchant (for sales transactions) or acquirer (for ATM and cash transactions) is registered in a country that is different from the country in which the issuer is registered. The fee is based on the USD value of transactions, converted at the daily BASE II settlement rate. IAF is a volume-based transaction charge levied in the case of cross-border transactions. IAF is levied on an acquirer when its merchant accepts a card issued by an issuer located in a different country in payment for goods and services. This additional transaction charge relates to the additional Treasury activities that Visa needs to perform, and the incremental FX risk it bears, in managing a global multi- currency settlement process.

Visa reports fees and charges on a daily and monthly basis. Individual transactions processing systems pass charges to an internal billing system, which consolidates them for reporting to clients. Visa also reports administrative and service charges, such as monthly VisaNet connection and VisaNet connection method access charges. Transaction processing charges are accumulated daily
and billed monthly. Charges settled by other Visa systems are included in the reports to provide a complete accounting of Visa charges for clients. IBS reports are produced monthly.
Reimbursement fees are listed on the daily reconciliation summary reports. Fees and charges assessed by Visa are reported on the daily settlement reports.

Monthly reports list transaction processing charges and administrative and service charges. Monthly reports include accumulated daily charges. The internal billing system reports all client-to-Visa charges on a monthly basis, accumulating daily charges for this billing. Categories reported include:
Transaction processing charges. Administrative and service charges.

Full service supports the following transactions for Visa in the POS environment. Authorization – Full service acquirers use an authorization transaction message when the final transaction amount is not known at the time of purchase. Manual Cash Disbursement – Manual cash disbursement is also called manual cash. ATM Cash Disbursement—ATM cash disbursement is the withdrawal of cash from an ATM. Preauthorization and Preauthorization Completion – This transaction is designed for merchant locations, such as fuel pumps, at which the purchase amount is not known at the time the cardholder initiates the transaction, but the merchant can provide the final transaction amount within two hours. Preauthorizations consist of an initial request message containing an estimated purchase amount followed by a completion message. The merchant is guaranteed payment if:

VisaNet receives the preauthorization completion message within two hours of the corresponding preauthorization request message. The amount in the completion message does not exceed the amount approved by the issuer.

Issuers can send a partial amount response to a preauthorization request when the full amount of a preauthorization request would exceed the cardholder's available funds or daily spending limit, but a lower amount could be approved. After two hours, issuers approve or decline transactions. Full service issuers processing POS transactions as 0100 authorizations can opt to receive 0220 preauthorization completion advices as downgraded 0120 advices. V.I.P. sends all 0120 preauthorization completion advices online to issuers set up to receive them.

Preauthorization completion messages cannot include PIN data (messages must not include field 52 and field 53); otherwise, V.I.P. rejects them. V.I.P  also does not allow network 0002 and network 0003 POS cancellation messages (Field 63.3 – Message Reason Code contains

V.I.P. rejects preauthorization completion messages received as 0200 messages with reject reason code 0599 (Consistency Error/Transaction Not Defined). Purchase – The purchase transaction is the basic POS transaction used for Visa POS processing. Variations of the purchase transaction include:
Purchase with cashback. Quasi-cash. Key-entered purchase. Purchase with address verification.

Purchase With Cashback – Cashback is a variation of the purchase transaction permitting the cardholder to get cash in addition to goods or services. Cashback is a domestic service available to participating Visa regions for their issuers, acquirers, and merchants. The VisaNet Cashback Service identifies the cashback amount separately in authorization messages and in settlement to allow issuers to make authorization decisions and to monitor cash activity for their cardholders, Clients can contact their Visa representatives for additional information on cashback features, controls, and availability. Quasi-Cash – Quasi-cash is a variation of the purchase transaction, used for the purchase of items directly convertible to cash, such as gaming chips and money orders. It is available for Visa POS and Interlink. VisaNet does not support American Express Quasi-cash transactions. Key-Entered Purchase – This transaction is a variation of the purchase transaction, used only for Visa POS transactions when the magnetic stripe on the card is not readable. Purchase With Address Verification – This transaction is used by such merchants as direct marketing firms and airlines to verify a cardholder's address as part of a purchase request. This transaction is available for Visa POS. Account Funding Transaction – This transaction is used to fund accounts such as brokerage accounts and online stored value cards, from a Visa debit or credit card. Original Credit Transaction – This transaction enables funds to be credited to Visa account numbers for a purpose other than refunding a Visa purchase. Deferred Clearing Purchase Transaction – This transaction is used by such merchants as hotels and car rental agencies when the full purchase amount is not known at the time of transaction authorization. This transaction, used only by Visa POS acquirers, involves an authorization request followed by a deferred clearing advice message. Merchandise Return – A merchandise return transaction enables merchants to credit the account of a Visa POS cardholder who returns merchandise. Balance Inquiry – Balance inquiry transactions enable cardholders to check their balances at stand- alone merchant terminals and at the point of sale.

If the issuer system cannot be reached, V.I.P. stand-in processing responds that issuer is not available. If the issuer is available and supports balance inquiries, VisaNet returns the account balance to the acquirer for display or for printing in the currency of the merchant or of the ATM. Issuers can optionally provide balance information in Visa POS purchase transaction responses. However, for an 0200 POS eFunds transactions (network 0029), the acquirer receives balance information in Field 54 – Additional Amounts regardless of the issuer's selected response options. (This processing does not apply to stand-alone balance inquiries.) ATM acquirers in the U.S. region must support balance inquiries; support of this transaction is optional for all other participants. PINs are required for full service 0200 POS balance inquiries. PINs may not be required if a chip card is being used in a full service 0100 POS balance inquiries. Address Verification Only (Visa POS) – This transaction is used by merchants like direct marketing firms and airlines to verify a cardholder's address before submitting a purchase transaction. Incremental Authorizations – Certain merchants, such as hotels, car rental companies, and airlines, initiate incremental authorization transactions when the final amount of the purchase is unknown. The incremental authorization contains an estimated amount that may vary significantly from the final transaction amount. When the merchant determines the final amount, it submits a supplemental, or incremental, authorization or a single authorization reversal if the purchase is cancelled. Endpoints must not decline incremental authorizations by treating them as duplicate transactions. In incremental authorization requests and their reversals, the field 11 and field 37 values match the corresponding values in the original authorization request message, and the field 62.2 value matches the corresponding value in the original authorization response message.
The following transactions are supported for Visa POS.

A reversal transaction, which is system-generated, can be initiated by an acquirer's host system or by V.I.P. Issuers and acquirers must match reversals to the corresponding financial transactions by using tracing data. There are two types of reversal transactions: reversal requests and reversal advices. Visa prefers reversal advices. Each must occur on the same calendar day as the transaction being reversed. Reversals must contain the same field 62.2 value present in the original response message. Acquirer-Initiated Reversals—POS acquirers and merchants use reversals, which are automatically generated by the client's system, to reverse approved authorizations or financial transactions not completed due to systems malfunctions or because the transactions timed out.
Acquirers must always generate an 0420 reversal if a transaction is not completed at the point of sale. Financial transactions are:
Manual cash disbursements. Purchases (all types). Merchandise returns.

Deferred clearing purchase transactions can also be reversed. Acquirers must not include field 35 or field 45 track data in non–U.S. 0220 deferred clearing advices for chip transactions; otherwise, V.I.P. will reject the transaction with reject code 0699—Invalid Presence of Track Data. VisaNet sends deferred clearing reversal advices to full service issuers for POS reversal transactions originated by BASE II acquirers. Issuers do not receive deferred clearing reversal advices during the same processing day as the original transactions. POS reversals can be used by:

A merchant, to reverse previous requests when responses are not received at the POS or received late. An acquirer, to reverse a prior request when the acquirer's system did not receive a response, received a late response, or is unable to forward an approval response to the POS. An acquirer, when a communications failure prevents transmission of a reversal request. The acquirer's system stores the reversal and forwards it to VisaNet when communications are restored.
V.I.P.-Initiated Reversals—V.I.P. initiates reversal advices in the following circumstances:

When a reversal cannot be forwarded to an issuer. In this case, V.I.P. responds to the acquirer and stores a reversal advice for later delivery to the issuer. When an approval response cannot be delivered to an acquirer. In this case, V.I.P. generates a reversal request for the issuer.
V.I.P. rejects reversal response messages without response code 00 in field 39 with Reject Code 0087 —Invalid Value or Reject Code  0590—Invalid Value (Not 00 or 55 When it Should Be).
The following transactions for Visa POS are used to correct errors occurring at the point of transaction or in a participant's system:
Adjustment (back-office) Dispute financial Dispute financial reversal Dispute response financial

Field 62.2 – Transaction Identifier must be present in back-office exception transactions; otherwise, the exceptions will be rejected with reason code 0153 or 0483. Visa issuers and acquirers must support exception-related transactions. Issuer systems must be able to create dispute financials and to receive adjustments and dispute response financials. Acquirer systems must be able to receive dispute financials and to create adjustments and dispute response financials. Because authorization is not required and exception-related transactions cannot be declined, V.I.P. always processes them as advices. In addition, Visa POS issuers must be able to create dispute financial reversals, and participating acquirers must be able to receive them. Each type of exception transaction is described in this section. Adjustment (Back-Office)—An acquirer initiates an adjustment to an original transaction to correct an error, such as an out-of-balance condition at the POS. The adjustment can be a debit or a credit (because the cardholder's account was charged less or more than the actual amount agreed on at the time of the transaction). VisaNet supports adjustment transactions for Visa transactions. Dispute Financial—A dispute financial transaction is used to credit a cardholder's (or customer's) account for the purchase amount under certain conditions. An issuer can initiate a dispute financial when:

A cardholder disputes a transaction. A cardholder asserts merchandise was returned but a merchandise credit transaction has not been received by the issuer. The issuer itself disputes a transaction. The issuer receives an unpostable debit adjustment from an acquirer.

VisaNet supports dispute financial transactions for Visa transactions. Dispute Financial Reversal—Visa issuers can initiate a dispute financial reversal to cancel a prior dispute financial transaction sent in error to the acquirer. Dispute Response Financial—Acquirers can initiate a dispute response financial transaction to debit a cardholder's account when the validity of a dispute financial can be disproved. The dispute response financial must be for the exact amount of the dispute financial. Dispute financials, dispute financial reversals, and dispute response financials must contain field 136 and field
137 if the original message contains them.

These transactions can be submitted by an issuer, an acquirer, or V.I.P. and do not require authorization. Visa issuers and acquirers must support fee-related transactions. There are two types of fee-related transactions for Visa and for Interlink, each of which has financial value:

Fee Collection – This transaction is used to collect miscellaneous fees. Funds Disbursement – This transaction is used to remit miscellaneous fees. Because authorization is not required and fee-related transactions cannot be declined, V.I.P. always processes them as advices.
VisaNet uses an automatic reconciliation advice to indicate the settlement day is closed and no more transactions will be processed for that settlement date.
